description: The OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) Model is a conceptual framework that standardizes computer network communication by dividing it into seven layers. Network devices like hubs, switches, and routers operate at specific layers to transmit data efficiently across networks.

sections.title: Introduction to the OSI Model
sections.description: Historical context of the OSI model and the format of data at its foundational layers.

historical_events.significance: Developed by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) to provide a standard framework for communication between different computer systems and network architectures.

key_associations.extra_info: Deals with raw data transmission over hardware like cables and signals.
Operates using MAC (Media Access Control) addresses.
Operates using IP addresses and handles routing.
Utilizes TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) and UDP (User Datagram Protocol).

sections.title: Key Layers of the OSI Model
sections.description: Functions and characteristics of the seven distinct layers of the OSI model.

key_concepts.explanation: The lowest layer responsible for transmitting raw bits (0s and 1s) over a physical communication medium such as fiber optic cables, copper wire, or wireless radio frequencies.
Ensures reliable node-to-node data transfer. It packages raw bits into frames and performs error detection and correction at the hardware level.
Responsible for determining the best physical path (routing) for data packets to travel from the source to the destination using logical addressing (IP).
Ensures the complete and reliable end-to-end delivery of data segments. It manages flow control and error recovery. It is often called the 'Heart of the OSI model'.

Session Layer (5) manages and terminates connections; Presentation Layer (6) handles data encryption, translation, and compression; Application Layer (7) provides network services directly to user applications (e.g., HTTP, FTP).

sections.title: Major Network Devices
sections.description: The operational mechanisms of hardware devices used to transmit data within and between networks.

key_concepts.explanation: A non-intelligent (dumb) central connection device that operates at the Physical Layer. It broadcasts received data to all its connected ports, which can cause network congestion and collisions.
An intelligent networking device that operates at the Data Link Layer. It uses a MAC address table to forward data frames exclusively to the specific target device, reducing network traffic.
A networking device operating at the Network Layer. It connects two or more different networks (like a LAN to the Internet) and forwards data packets between them using IP addresses.
Stands for Modulator-Demodulator. It converts digital signals from a computer into analog signals for transmission over telephone or cable lines, and vice versa.

sections.description: Mapping specific network hardware devices to their corresponding operating layers in the OSI model.

key_associations.extra_info: A repeater is used specifically to regenerate and amplify weak signals over long distances.
Both devices rely on hardware addresses (MAC addresses) to direct traffic within a local network.
Relies on logical addresses (IP addresses) to route data across wide area networks.
A complex device or software that connects two completely dissimilar networks, acting as a protocol translator.

sections.title: Important Facts for Exams
sections.description: Crucial one-liner facts related to the OSI model, IP addresses, and network devices.

important_facts.fact: A popular mnemonic to remember the 7 OSI layers from bottom (1) to top (7) is: 'Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away' (Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application).
A MAC Address is a unique 48-bit physical address that is hard-coded onto the Network Interface Card (NIC) by the manufacturer.
An IPv4 Address is a 32-bit logical address divided into four octets, whereas the newer IPv6 format is a 128-bit address.
A Switch operates in full-duplex mode (can send and receive data simultaneously), whereas a Hub only operates in half-duplex mode.
The Application Layer is the layer closest to the end-user, meaning both the OSI application layer and the user interact directly with the software application.
